etymology: Latin gentilis (of the same family); the disposition of one who deals tenderly because the other belongs to him.
biblical_def: Biblical gentleness is the strong man's deliberate softness toward those weaker than himself — not weakness but bridled strength. Galatians 5 lists it as fruit of the Spirit; Paul commands the Philippians to let theirs be known unto all men; Christ commends Himself to the laboring crowd as meek and lowly in heart.
webster_summary: Softness of manner; mildness; sweetness of disposition; the disposition that yields gracefully to others.
webster_full: GENTLENESS, n. Softness of manner; mildness; sweetness of disposition; meekness; tenderness.

In Scripture, gentleness is consistently the demeanor of strength deliberately restrained — the king who does not need to crush, the father who does not need to shout, the apostle who deals with the church as a nurse with her own children (1 Thess 2:7).
scriptures: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith.
Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand.
But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children.
Now I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ.
corruption_summary: Modern culture mistakes gentleness for softness; Scripture treats it as the strongest man's deliberate restraint.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ is gentle in Matthew 11:29 because He is meek and lowly in heart. The point is not that He cannot bring force; the point is that He chooses not to. Gentleness is the King's self-restraint.

The household, the workplace, the Marine all need this version of the virtue: power present but bridled, capacity to crush, choosing not to crush. Recover the strong-restraint sense and gentleness becomes admirable again.
roots_summary: Greek has multiple words; Galatians 5 uses chrēstotēs, useful kindness.
roots_lines: Greek chrēstotēs — useful goodness, kindness; the fruit-of-the-Spirit word.
Greek epieikeia — reasonable yielding, ‘moderation’ (Phil 4:5); the bridled strength.
usage: Gentleness is power present, choosing not to crush.
The strong man is gentle on purpose.
Let your moderation be known unto all men — that is bridled strength gone public.

etymology: Old Norse m&juki (soft, mild); but in Greek praotēs names a war-horse's reined power — not weakness, but harness.
biblical_def: Biblical meekness is reined power. The Greek praotēs in classical use named a war-horse trained to obey the rider's lightest touch — full strength under perfect control. Christ called Himself meek and lowly, and Moses (Num 12:3) is named the meekest man on earth — while leading two million people through a wilderness.
webster_summary: Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; submission to the divine will without murmuring or peevishness.
webster_full: MEEKNESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries and provocations.
Webster captures the ‘mildness’ sense; the Greek captures the ‘harnessed strength’ sense. Both are needed; modern English has lost the second.
scriptures: Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth.
Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart.
Restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
corruption_summary: Modern English equates meek with timid, doormat, weak; the Greek means a war-horse harnessed.
corruption_paragraphs: Moses, the meekest man on earth (Num 12:3), led two million through a desert and confronted Pharaoh to his face. Christ, the meek and lowly, made a whip of cords and cleared the temple. Meekness in Scripture has nothing to do with timidity.

Recover the war-horse picture and Matthew 5:5 stops sounding sentimental: blessed are the meek — for they shall inherit the earth. The earth goes to those whose strength obeys the Rider, not to those who have no strength at all.
roots_summary: Greek praotēs is the technical term for the trained war-horse's controllable power.
roots_lines: Greek praotēs / prautēs — meekness; in classical Greek used of horses broken to harness.
Note: paired in 1 Peter 3:4 with quiet as the inner ornament ‘of great price in the sight of God’.
usage: Meekness is a war-horse harnessed.
Moses was the meekest man on earth and led two million through a desert.
The earth goes to those whose strength obeys the Rider.

etymology: Latin patientia, from patior (to suffer, to bear). The capacity to remain under without breaking.
biblical_def: Biblical patience is the capacity to remain under pressure without breaking — whether that pressure is hostile (longsuffering toward people) or simply long (endurance under God's timing). The Greek distinguishes the two: makrothumia for slow-fuse with persons, hypomonē for steadfast endurance under circumstance.
webster_summary: The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation or other evil, with a calm, unruffled temper.
webster_full: PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation, or other evil with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring or fretfulness.
Two Greek words underlie the New Testament concept: makrothumia (long-temperedness) and hypomonē (remaining-under). Together they cover patience with people and patience with God's timing.
scriptures: But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.
Tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope.
Let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us.
The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward.
corruption_summary: Modern usage flattens patience to a personality trait; Scripture treats it as a hard-won discipline tested in real fire.
corruption_paragraphs: James 1:4 says patience has work to do — let patience have her perfect work. The point is not that some people are by nature patient. The point is that the Spirit's patience is forged in tribulation (Rom 5:3) and produces character.
The household and the believer who run the race with hypomonē (Heb 12:1) outrun those whose only patience is temperamental. Real patience can be acquired; temperamental calm cannot stand a real fire.
roots_summary: Two Greek words carry the meaning, with different fields of application.
roots_lines: Greek makrothumia — long-temperedness; patience with persons.
Greek hypomonē — remaining-under; endurance through circumstance.
usage: Tribulation produces patience — not the other way around.
Long-temperedness with people; remaining-under with circumstances.
Run the race with hypomonē; sprinters do not finish.

etymology: Latin gaudium; the deep, settled gladness of soul that does not require pleasant circumstance.
biblical_def: Biblical joy is the deep, settled gladness of soul that does not depend on circumstance. It is the second fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22), the strength of the rebuilders in Nehemiah's day (the joy of the LORD is your strength), and the climax of the angel's nativity announcement: good tidings of great joy. Distinct from happiness, which depends on what happens.
webster_summary: Excitement of pleasurable feeling caused by some good or supposed good; happiness; gladness.
webster_full: JOY, n. Webster gives both the surface sense (delight at present good) and the deeper sense (settled gladness of soul).
Scripture's joy is consistently the deeper sense — the saint's gladness that survives loss, persecution, and waiting (Hab 3:17-18; Acts 5:41; James 1:2).
scriptures: The joy of the LORD is your strength.
Although the fig tree shall not blossom... yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
Behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.
These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often conflates joy with positive emotion; Scripture insists it is a fruit, not a mood.
corruption_paragraphs: Habakkuk 3:17-18 is the test case. Crops fail, herds die, fields lie barren — yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. Joy holds when happiness is impossible.

John 15:11 gives the source: Christ's own joy implanted in the saint. It does not depend on the saint's emotional weather; it depends on Christ's indwelling. Cultivated like fruit, not chased like a feeling.
roots_summary: Hebrew has multiple words for joy, gladness, exultation; Greek chara is the New Testament noun.
roots_lines: Hebrew simchah — gladness, festive joy.
Greek chara — joy; cognate with charis (grace) — the joy that springs from grace given.
usage: Joy is fruit, not mood.
The joy of the LORD is your strength — rebuilding requires it.
Rejoice in the LORD when the fig tree fails; that is joy proven.

etymology: Latin pax; but the deeper word is Hebrew shalom — wholeness, completeness, well-ordered life.
biblical_def: Biblical peace is not the absence of conflict; it is the presence of right order. Hebrew shalom means wholeness, completeness, well-being — the integrated state of a life or community in which everything is in its proper place. Greek eirēnē carries the same depth: peace with God (Rom 5:1), peace among believers (Eph 4:3), and the peace of God that surpasses understanding (Phil 4:7).
webster_summary: A state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from disturbance; concord; amity; harmony.
webster_full: PEACE, n. Webster lists eleven distinct senses, from international peace to peace of conscience to the peace of God.

Scripture's peace runs deeper than any one of them. Shalom is the state where every relationship — with God, self, neighbor, creation — is rightly ordered. Not the absence of conflict; the presence of right order.
scriptures: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you.
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee.
corruption_summary: Modern peace is often the absence of friction; biblical peace is the presence of right order. The two are not the same.
corruption_paragraphs: A household can be conflict-free and not at peace — if the conflict-avoidance is achieved by silence, screens, and parallel orbits. Shalom requires the harder work of relational rightness, not just the absence of disturbance.

John 14:27 makes the distinction explicit: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. The world's peace is fragile, circumstantial, externally enforced. Christ's peace survives storms because it is anchored elsewhere.
roots_summary: Hebrew and Greek both carry depth far beyond English ‘quiet’.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalom — wholeness, completeness, well-being, peace.
Greek eirēnē — peace; in the New Testament a near-equivalent of shalom, especially in Pauline benedictions.
usage: Peace is right order, not silenced conflict.
Shalom in the household is harder than household quiet.
Christ's peace is not the world's; do not confuse the two.

etymology: Latin merces (reward, recompense), borrowed into Old French; in Christian usage, the unmerited compassion that withholds deserved judgment and supplies undeserved help.
biblical_def: Biblical mercy is loving-kindness directed at the miserable. Hebrew chesed covers covenant loyalty extended even when undeserved; Greek eleos covers compassion stooping to the wounded. Christ's ministry was a continual flow of such mercy: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice.
webster_summary: That benevolence, mildness, or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to forbear punishment.
webster_full: MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness, or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves.

In Scripture, mercy is one of the great divine attributes; God is described as plenteous in mercy, and Christ's entire earthly ministry is described as a flow of healing, forgiving, and feeding mercies toward the helpless.
scriptures: For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
He shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often pairs mercy with leniency only; Scripture pairs it with compassion that costs the helper to give it.
corruption_paragraphs: The Good Samaritan's mercy in Luke 10 cost him a donkey, a delay, and two pence. It was not vague good feeling; it was concrete help paid for. Mercy in Scripture always costs the merciful man something.
James 2:13 makes the symmetry sharp: he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy. The merciful obtain mercy; the unmerciful do not. The household that practices mercy receives it.
roots_summary: Hebrew and Greek both have a word for the loving-kindness directed at the wretched.
roots_lines: Hebrew chesed — covenant loyalty, loving-kindness, mercy; one of the great Old Testament words for God's character.
Greek eleos — compassion, mercy; the New Testament's standard term.
usage: Mercy is concrete; it costs the merciful something.
Blessed are the merciful, for they obtain mercy — the symmetry of James 2.
I will have mercy, and not sacrifice — that ranks the priorities.

etymology: Old English cynd (kin, of one's own family); kindness is treatment as kin — the disposition that meets the other as one's own.
biblical_def: Biblical kindness is the disposition that treats the other as one's own kin. Hebrew chesed covers it; Greek chrēstotēs names it as fruit of the Spirit. The deepest theological use: the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared — in the incarnation itself.
webster_summary: Good will; benevolence; that temper or disposition which delights in contributing to the happiness of others.
webster_full: KINDNESS, n. Good will; benevolence; that temper or disposition which delights in contributing to the happiness of others.

The English word preserves its old root: kindness is the way of treating someone as of one's own kind. The Christian extension turns every neighbor and even every stranger into kin worth treating kindly.
scriptures: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness.
But after that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared.
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity.
corruption_summary: Modern English uses ‘kind’ for the merely pleasant; biblical kindness has a covenantal weight — it treats the other as kin.
corruption_paragraphs: Pleasant is cheap; kindness as covenant-treatment is not. Ephesians 4:32 grounds it in God's kindness toward us — even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you. The household practices kindness because it has received kindness, and at the same depth.

Titus 3:4 makes kindness the very name for what God did at the incarnation: His kindness appeared. The recovery of biblical kindness restores its weight: it is more than a smile, less than mercy, and unmistakably divine in its origin.
roots_summary: Greek chrēstotēs is the fruit-of-Spirit word.
roots_lines: Greek chrēstotēs — useful kindness, goodness; cognate with chrēstos (good, kind, useful).
Note: same root as Christos (Christ); some early hearers heard Chrēstos as a near-pun on the Lord's title.
usage: Kindness treats the other as kin.
Be ye kind one to another — the household's baseline.
God's kindness appeared in flesh; ours follows the pattern.

etymology: Latin modestia, from modus (measure). The discipline of staying within proper measure — in dress, speech, and self-presentation.
biblical_def: Biblical modesty is the discipline of measure — in apparel, speech, and self-presentation. Paul commands it of women adorning themselves with shamefacedness and sobriety; Peter reaches the same point with not the outward adorning... but the hidden man of the heart. Modesty is broader than dress, but it is not less.
webster_summary: Restraint of the senses, of the appetites, of the passions, especially in dress and bearing; chastity; a becoming reserve.
webster_full: MODESTY, n. Restraint of the senses, of the appetites, of the passions; chastity; a becoming reserve in carriage, conversation, and dress.
Webster captures the breadth: modesty is not a dress code only; it is a disposition that governs how one carries oneself in public, how one speaks, what one wears, and what one calls attention to.
scriptures: In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array.
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit.
As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity reduces modesty to a checklist of garment lengths; Scripture treats it as a measured way of being in the world.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Timothy 2:9-10 connects modest apparel to good works — the woman's adornment is finally ethical, not sartorial. 1 Peter 3:3-4 connects it to the heart — the hidden person, the meek and quiet spirit.

Recovering modesty as measure rather than checklist changes the conversation. The question is not how short or how high; it is whether the person's presentation calls measured attention or excessive attention. The answer governs men and women alike.
roots_summary: Greek has a specific word for the becoming reserve in apparel and bearing.
roots_lines: Greek kosmios (1 Tim 2:9) — orderly, well-arranged; modest in the broader sense.
Greek aidos — reverence, modesty, the ‘shamefacedness’ of 1 Tim 2:9; the disposition that recoils from impropriety.
usage: Modesty is measure, not list.
The hidden man of the heart is the deepest adorning.
A jewel of gold in a swine's snout — Solomon's warning still stands.

etymology: Latin humilitas, from humus (the ground); the disposition of one who knows where his body comes from.
biblical_def: Biblical humility is the right estimate of one's self before God — not falsely low, not falsely high, but accurate. Christ supplies the great example in Philippians 2: He made himself of no reputation, took on flesh, became obedient to death. The saint's humility is the imprint of His.
webster_summary: Freedom from pride and arrogance; humbleness of mind; a modest estimate of one's own worth; a right estimate of self before God.
webster_full: HUMILITY, n. Freedom from pride and arrogance; humbleness of mind; a modest estimate of one's own worth.

Webster adds the religious sense: ‘in theology, humility consists in lowliness of mind; a deep sense of one's own unworthiness in the sight of God.’ The religious sense is the deeper one; the others depend on it.
scriptures: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity confuses humility with low self-esteem; biblical humility is accurate self-estimate before God, which usually feels much lower than self-esteem culture allows but never falsely so.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ in Philippians 2 did not pretend to be smaller than He was; He was the eternal Son. He humbled Himself by taking what was lower than His station — flesh, servanthood, death. The pattern is humility as voluntary descent, not pretended insignificance.

James 4:10 and 1 Peter 5:6 both pair humility with subsequent exaltation by God. Humility is therefore not self-erasure; it is positioning oneself so that God can lift, on His own timing. Humble yourselves... he shall lift you up.
roots_summary: Hebrew and Greek both have words rooted in lowness of station.
roots_lines: Hebrew anavah — humility, meekness; the disposition of the anav (humble one).
Greek tapeinophrosynē — literally lowliness of mind; the New Testament's standard term.
usage: Humility is accurate self-estimate, not self-erasure.
Humble yourselves; He will lift you up.
Christ humbled Himself by descent, not by pretense.

etymology: Latin aequus (equal, level) plus animus (mind, spirit). Levelness of mind in shifting circumstance.
biblical_def: Equanimity is settled levelness of mind in shifting circumstance. Paul names it without using the word: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content (Phil 4:11). Job displays it under loss: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD. Equanimity is the mark of a soul whose center is not in the surrounding weather.
webster_summary: Evenness of mind; that calm temper or firmness of mind which is not easily elated or depressed.
webster_full: EQUANIMITY, n. Evenness of mind; that calm temper or firmness of mind which is not easily elated or depressed in prosperity or adversity.
Equanimity is closely related to patience but distinct from it: patience endures; equanimity remains level, neither over-elevated by good news nor crushed by bad.
scriptures: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry.
Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often values emotional intensity; equanimity looks suspiciously flat to a culture trained on highs and lows.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul says he learned it. Equanimity is not temperament; it is achievement. The man who has learned to be abased and to abound has trained the soul to a single level, anchored elsewhere than in the bank account or the mood.

Equanimity is not stoicism — the saint still rejoices, still grieves. But the rejoicing does not lift him into pride and the grief does not drop him into despair. The center holds because it is in Christ, not in circumstance.
roots_summary: The Latin compound is the cleanest English window into the concept.
roots_lines: Latin aequus (equal, level) plus animus (mind) — level-mindedness.
Note: closely related to Greek autarkeia (self-sufficiency, contentment) of Phil 4:11 — the contentment that is sufficient in itself because it is anchored in God.
usage: Equanimity is learned, not given.
The level mind anchors elsewhere than the weather.
Job's blessing under loss is equanimity made audible.

etymology: Greek agapē, the New Testament's technical term for self-giving covenant love — not erotic, not familial, not affectionate, but willed.
biblical_def: Agape is the New Testament's great word for love — the willed, self-giving, covenant-keeping love that originates in God and is poured out in the saint by the Spirit. Distinct from eros (erotic), philia (friendly affection), and storgē (familial). Agape is the love commanded toward enemies, neighbors, and God Himself.
webster_summary: (Greek loanword.) Self-giving covenant love; the New Testament's primary word for the love of God toward man and the love commanded among believers.
webster_full: Webster 1828 does not enter agape; the term entered popular English usage in the 20th century with the recovery of Greek-distinction theology.

Greek had four primary love-words: eros (passionate / desiring), philia (friendship / affection), storgē (familial), and agapē (willed, self-giving). The New Testament authors elected agapē as their primary love-word almost entirely — raising the bar for what Christian love means.
scriptures: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son.
The love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.
He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.
Love your enemies, bless them that curse you.
corruption_summary: ‘Love’ in modern English collapses all four Greek words into one; the New Testament's sharpness disappears.
corruption_paragraphs: When John writes God is love, he uses agapē. When Christ commands love your enemies, He uses agapē. When Paul says love is the greatest (1 Cor 13:13), he uses agapē. The New Testament is making a specific claim: a particular kind of love — willed, self-giving, covenantal — is the heart of God and the standard for the saint.

Modern English ‘love’ covers Bible love, romantic love, family love, and casual liking, all with one word. The result is that biblical love-commands feel impossible (because we read them through erotic or affectionate lenses) when in fact they are willed — we can decide to act in agape even when we do not feel philia.
roots_summary: One Greek word, distinct from three others, carries the New Testament's primary love-meaning.
roots_lines: Greek agapē — willed, covenant, self-giving love.
Note: eros does not appear in the New Testament; philia appears occasionally; storgē appears only in the negative compound astorgos (without natural affection).
usage: Agape is willed; you do not have to feel it to do it.
God is love — agape, specifically.
Love your enemies is a command; therefore the love is choosable.

etymology: Latin reverentia, from revereri (to stand in awe of). The settled inner disposition of awe before God, parents, elders, and holy things.
biblical_def: Biblical reverence is the settled inner posture of awe before God, His Name, His house, His Word, His messengers, and His ordained authorities. Hebrews commands it as the New Covenant's appropriate response to receiving an unshakable kingdom: let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear.
webster_summary: Fear mingled with respect and esteem; a feeling of profound respect, often bordering on awe.
webster_full: REVERENCE, n. Fear mingled with respect and esteem; veneration; the disposition that recognizes superior worth or holiness and responds with awe.

Scripture commands reverence in five spheres: toward God Himself (Heb 12:28), toward His sanctuary (Lev 19:30), toward parents (Lev 19:3), toward elders / authority (1 Pet 2:17), and toward the husband (Eph 5:33).
scriptures: Let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear.
Ye shall keep my sabbaths, and reverence my sanctuary: I am the LORD.
And the wife see that she reverence her husband.
Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected us, and we gave them reverence.
corruption_summary: Modern egalitarian culture is allergic to reverence; Scripture commands it deliberately and broadly.
corruption_paragraphs: Reverence cuts against the modern grain. The democratic instinct is that nothing and no one deserves a posture of awe. Scripture insists on the opposite: God deserves it, His sanctuary asks for it, parents earn it, husbands receive it, and the saints owe it.

The recovery is not the recovery of inequality; it is the recovery of recognized weight. Some persons and some places are heavy in the Lord's economy. The saint who does not learn to feel that weight will treat everything as level — and miss most of what Scripture commands.
roots_summary: Greek and Hebrew both have words for awe-with-respect, distinct from raw fear.
roots_lines: Hebrew yare — to fear, reverence; behind ‘the fear of the LORD’.
Greek eulabeia — cautious devout reverence; the word in Hebrews 12:28.
usage: Reverence is recognized weight, not slavish fear.
Let us serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear.
The husband is to be reverenced; the wife is to be loved as Christ loves the church.

etymology: Latin compassio, from com- (with) plus pati (suffer). To suffer with another.
biblical_def: Biblical compassion is the disposition that suffers with another's suffering — not pity from a distance but visceral, embodied joining. The Greek splanchnizomai describes Christ as moved in the bowels at the sight of the harassed crowd, the leper, the blind, the bereaved widow. Compassion in Scripture is always followed by action.
webster_summary: A suffering with another; pity; commiseration; sympathy of pain or sorrow.
webster_full: COMPASSION, n. A suffering with another; pity; that sentiment of the heart which is excited by the suffering or distress of another.

The Greek splanchnizomai (used twelve times in the Synoptic Gospels of Jesus) is more visceral: literally moved in the bowels, an internal stirring that propels the compassionate man toward the suffering one.
scriptures: But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.
And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him, and said unto him, I will; be thou clean.
And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not.
Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind.
corruption_summary: Modern compassion is often performative and at distance; Scripture's compassion is visceral and immediate, always producing concrete help.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's compassion in the Gospels is consistently followed by an action: He healed, He fed, He raised, He taught, He touched the leper. The internal movement always produced an external response. There is no scene of distant Christly pity.

The household's compassion follows the same pattern. If the bowels are moved but no hand goes out, the compassion is incomplete. If a hand goes out without the inner movement, the help is mechanical. Scripture asks for both.
roots_summary: Greek has the visceral verb; Hebrew uses the related rachamim (womb-mercies).
roots_lines: Greek splanchnizomai — to be moved in the inward parts; the New Testament's most visceral compassion verb.
Hebrew rachamim — tender mercies, compassions; cognate with rechem (womb).
usage: Compassion in Scripture is always followed by action.
Bowels moved without hand extended is incomplete.
Hand extended without bowels moved is mechanical.

etymology: Old English milde, soft, gentle; the disposition that does not aggravate.
biblical_def: Mildness is the saintly disposition that does not aggravate — soft of word, slow of temper, deliberate in handling those whose nerves are already raw. Paul commands it of pastors: not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler. Mildness is one of the characteristic temperaments of those entrusted with souls.
webster_summary: Softness; tenderness; mercy; gentleness of temper.
webster_full: MILDNESS, n. Softness; tenderness; mercy; gentleness of temper; clemency.

Closely related to gentleness, but emphasizing the temperamental rather than the situational: gentleness chooses to deal softly in a moment, mildness is the disposition that prefers softness as a default.
scriptures: Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous.
To speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle, shewing all meekness unto all men.
And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient.
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.
corruption_summary: Modern Christian leadership culture sometimes prizes provocation; the New Testament prizes mildness in those who handle souls.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's pastor-qualifications repeatedly forbid the brawler, the striker, the contentious. The man entrusted with souls must be by temperament one who does not aggravate. This is not a personality test; it is the New Testament's assumption about who handles God's people.

The household needs the same temperament. A father, mother, husband, wife, or older sibling whose default is mildness raises a household differently than one whose default is reaction. The Spirit cultivates mildness; the saint can ask Him for it.
roots_summary: Greek epieikēs covers reasonable, equitable mildness.
roots_lines: Greek epieikēs — reasonable, equitable, mild; the ‘moderation’ of Phil 4:5 and the ‘gentle’ of 1 Tim 3:3.
Note: closely related to prautēs (meekness) but emphasizing the disposition's reasonableness.
usage: Mildness is the disposition that does not aggravate.
The pastor must be by temperament a mild man.
Slow to speak, slow to wrath — James 1:19 is mildness on the tongue.

etymology: Latin generosus (of noble birth); the disposition of one who gives because the family of God's children is large.
biblical_def: Biblical generosity is the open-handed disposition of one who gives because God has given. Paul says God loveth a cheerful giver; Christ said it is more blessed to give than to receive; the early church in Acts 4 is described in cosmic terms: great grace was upon them all... neither was there any among them that lacked. Generosity is grace flowing through the saint into the church and the world.
webster_summary: Liberality in giving; munificence; readiness to bestow benefits.
webster_full: GENEROSITY, n. Liberality in principle; a disposition to give liberally or to bestow favors; the noble greatness of mind that confers favors without expecting return.
Scripture treats generosity as grace flowing outward: God gives, the saint receives, the saint gives. The chain is broken only when the saint refuses to be a conduit.
scriptures: It is more blessed to give than to receive.
Neither was there any among them that lacked: for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold.
The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity sometimes treats generosity as a tax; Scripture treats it as a temperament — the saint who has received grace cannot help but give.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 4 describes generosity as great grace was upon them all — first divine grace upon the church, then human generosity flowing from it. Generosity in Scripture is always downstream of grace received.

The household that wants to grow in generosity does not start with the budget; it starts with the heart that has received from God. Freely ye have received, freely give (Mt 10:8). When the receiving is fresh, the giving is easy.
roots_summary: Greek haplotēs (singleness, generosity) and charis (grace, gift) carry the meaning.
roots_lines: Greek haplotēs — singleness, simplicity, generosity; an open-handedness that does not calculate.
Note: 2 Cor 8-9 is the New Testament's most extended treatment of giving; it uses charis (grace) as the dominant word.
usage: Generosity is grace flowing through the saint.
Freely received, freely given — the chain is unbroken.
God loves a cheerful giver, not a calculating one.

etymology: Old French guile (deceit), with negative ending. The state of being without guile — transparent, undeceiving.
biblical_def: Guilelessness is the disposition of one who does not deceive. Christ commended Nathanael with one of His highest commendations: behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile. Peter applies the same word to Christ Himself: who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth. Guilelessness is not naive simplicity; it is moral transparency.
webster_summary: Without deceit; honest, transparent in word and dealing.
webster_full: GUILE, n. Craft; cunning; artifice; duplicity; deceit; usually in a bad sense.
Guilelessness is the negation: the disposition free from craft, cunning, and duplicity. Christ applied it to Nathanael at first meeting; Peter applied it to Christ across His whole life.
scriptures: Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!
Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.
Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings.
Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile.
corruption_summary: Our culture rewards strategic communication, image-management, and brand-curation; the saint is called to guilelessness, which looks suspiciously naive.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 32:2 makes guile the opposite of blessedness in the spirit. 1 Peter 2:1 lists guile alongside malice and hypocrisy as things to be laid aside on conversion. The saint is to be transparent — words match meanings, public matches private, presented self matches actual self.

Modern social life rewards the opposite: curated image, strategic disclosure, calculated impression. The saint's guilelessness will look strange in such a context. Christ called it the highest commendation.
roots_summary: Greek dolos (bait, deceit) is the term Peter uses; the negation is the virtue.
roots_lines: Greek dolos — bait, deceit, treachery; the word in 1 Peter 2:1, 22.
Note: cognate with doloō (to bait, ensnare); guile is fish-hook morality.
usage: Guilelessness is moral transparency, not naive simplicity.
An Israelite indeed in whom is no guile — the highest commendation at first meeting.
Words match meanings; public matches private; that is the saint's standard.

etymology: Old English single (one) plus mind. The state of being undivided in attention or aim — the eye single in Christ's sense.
biblical_def: Single-minded names the saint whose attention, allegiance, and aim are undivided. Christ taught it with the figure of the single eye — the eye that fixes on one object and is therefore filled with light. James contrasts it with the double-minded man, unstable in all his ways. Single-mindedness is wholeness of orientation.
webster_summary: Having or characterized by a single purpose; undivided in attention or aim.
webster_full: Webster: single — “simple; undivided; uncompounded.”
Christ's ‘if therefore thine eye be single’ (Mt 6:22) names a focus that gathers light; James' dipsychos (double-souled) names the man who tries to focus on two and gathers neither.
scriptures: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.
This one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before.
One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after.
corruption_summary: Modern life multiplies attention by design; single-mindedness is the discipline of subtracting it.
corruption_paragraphs: James calls double-mindedness instability. The split self cannot stand: it leans toward God on Sunday and toward the world Monday through Saturday, and over time the leaning toward the world wins.

Recovery is subtraction. Psalm 27:4's one thing; Philippians 3:13's this one thing I do. The household, the believer, and the leader all need a deliberate practice of subtracting until the eye is single again.
roots_summary: Greek haplous (single, simple) and dipsychos (double-souled) are the New Testament's pair.
roots_lines: Greek haplous — single, simple, sound (Mt 6:22).
Greek dipsychos — double-souled, James' coinage for the divided man (Jas 1:8; 4:8).
usage: Single-mindedness is subtraction, not concentration.
If thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
The double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.

etymology: Old English godlic plus fær. The fear that is appropriate before God — reverence with weight, distinct from terror.
biblical_def: Godly fear is the reverent dread proper to a creature before the Holy God — not slavish terror, not casual familiarity, but the weight of recognized holiness. Hebrews calls it the manner of acceptable service: let us serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear. Solomon calls the fear of the LORD the beginning of wisdom.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The reverent awe of God appropriate to the creature's relation to the Creator.
webster_full: Webster: fear — in religious sense, “a kind of awe; reverence; veneration.”
Scripture distinguishes godly fear (proper reverence) from worldly fear (anxiety, dread of man, panic). Two different Hebrew and Greek words sometimes overlap; context distinguishes them.
scriptures: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear.
Who in the days of his flesh... was heard in that he feared.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity flinches at fear-of-the-LORD vocabulary; Scripture insists it is the beginning of wisdom and the proper manner of acceptable service.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors flank godly fear. The first softens it into vague respect — God-as-grandfather, no real weight. The second hardens it into terror — God-as-tyrant, no relationship. Scripture refuses both: godly fear is reverence with weight, perfectly compatible with the saint's confidence at the throne of grace (Heb 4:16).
Christ Himself, in Hebrews 5:7, was heard in that he feared. The Son of God prayed in godly fear. The saint who never feels the weight of holiness has not yet met the God of Hebrews.
roots_summary: Hebrew yirat YHWH (fear of YHWH) is the great Old Testament technical term.
roots_lines: Hebrew yirat YHWH — the fear of the LORD; the beginning of wisdom.
Greek eulabeia — cautious devout reverence; the word in Hebrews 5:7 of Christ Himself.
usage: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom — not its end, but its beginning.
Christ Himself was heard in that He feared.
Reverence with weight is the manner of acceptable service.

etymology: Old English trēowth (faithful, true) with abstract ending. The disposition that speaks what is.
biblical_def: Truthfulness is the saint's disposition of speaking and dealing in accordance with what is. Paul commands the church: putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour. Christ called Himself the truth; the saint's tongue is to bear the same family resemblance.
webster_summary: Veracity; the quality of being truthful; habit of speaking truth.
webster_full: TRUTH, n. Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be.

Truthfulness is the habituated disposition: the saint who speaks truth not by accident but by character. Scripture commands it positively (Eph 4:25), prohibits its opposite (Col 3:9), and grounds it in Christ Himself (Jn 14:6).
scriptures: Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds.
I am the way, the truth, and the life.
These are the things that ye shall do; Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour.
corruption_summary: Modern social life rewards strategic dishonesty — spin, image, polite untruth. Scripture flatly forbids all of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 4:25 grounds truthfulness in body-life: we are members one of another. Lying within the body of Christ is the equivalent of an organ deceiving the rest of the body about its condition — a recipe for collapse.

Recovery is direct. Speak what is. Decline to spin. Match words to meanings. Refuse the social rewards of the polite lie. The saint's tongue is supposed to look like Christ's, who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth (1 Pet 2:22).
roots_summary: Hebrew emet (firmness, truth) and Greek aletheia (truth, reality) carry the meaning.
roots_lines: Hebrew emet — firmness, truth, faithfulness; cognate with amen.
Greek alētheia — truth, reality, that which is unconcealed.
usage: Speak every man truth with his neighbor — Paul does not soften it.
We are members one of another; lies in the body are organs deceiving each other.
Christ's tongue had no guile; ours follow the pattern.

etymology: Latin puritas (cleanness) plus the heart as the inner seat of will and affection.
biblical_def: Purity of heart is the inner cleanness Christ commends in the sixth Beatitude: blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Distinct from ritual purity, it is the state of an inner life undivided by competing loves and uncluttered by hidden sin — the prerequisite, Christ says, for vision of God.
webster_summary: Cleanness of the inward seat of will, thought, and affection; freedom from corruption and from divided loves.
webster_full: PURITY, n. Freedom from any sinister or improper views; freedom from foreign admixture or moral defilement.
Of the heart specifically: the inward state in which God's claim is undivided, sin is unhidden, and the affections are not bonded to lesser things.
scriptures: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity.
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often reduces purity to sexual ethics; Scripture covers will, thought, affection, and motive together.
corruption_paragraphs: The Beatitude promises sight of God. The condition is purity of heart — broader than sexual purity, though it includes it. The pure-hearted have nothing hidden, no rival affections enthroned, no double-mindedness. They see God because nothing in them is in the way.
Recovery requires David's prayer (Ps 51:10): create in me a clean heart, O God. The saint cannot manufacture purity; he can ask. The Spirit cleanses what we name and surrender.
roots_summary: Greek katharos (clean, pure) and Hebrew tahor (clean, ritually pure).
roots_lines: Greek katharos — clean, pure; behind katharsis in modern English.
Hebrew tahor — clean, pure; ritual and moral cleanness alike.
usage: The pure in heart see God; that is the promise.
Purity is broader than sexual; it covers every hidden corner.
Create in me a clean heart, O God — David's prayer remains the saint's.

etymology: Old English hearm (injury) plus negative ending. The disposition that does no injury — the dove without venom.
biblical_def: Harmlessness is the saint's disposition of doing no injury — harmless as doves, in Christ's instruction to the apostles. Paul names the church to be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation. The picture is of those who carry no venom into the world's ecosystem.
webster_summary: Free from harm; not causing injury or evil; innocent in conduct.
webster_full: HARMLESS, adj. Free from harm; not causing or inflicting injury; innocent.
Greek akeraios (Mt 10:16; Phil 2:15) means unmixed, unalloyed — without admixture of poison; the dove without venom.
scriptures: Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation.
I would have you wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil.
For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners.
corruption_summary: Modern Christian discourse often valorizes the verbal ‘owning’ of opponents; Christ commanded harmlessness, even toward wolves.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's instruction in Matthew 10:16 is striking: in the midst of wolves, be wise as serpents (perceive the danger) and harmless as doves (carry no venom). The combination is rare and exact.

Modern social media incentivizes the opposite: maximum venom, minimum wisdom. The saint who recovers Christ's combination becomes useful to the kingdom in proportion to how rare the combination has become.
roots_summary: Greek akeraios names what is unmixed and unalloyed.
roots_lines: Greek akeraios — unmixed, pure, without admixture of evil; the ‘harmless’ of Mt 10:16 and Phil 2:15.
Note: Hebrews 7:26 uses akakos (without evil) of Christ — harmless in the deepest moral sense.
usage: Wise as serpents, harmless as doves — both halves required.
The saint carries no venom into the world's ecosystem.
Christ Himself was holy, harmless, undefiled.

etymology: Latin precari (to ask, beseech) with English abstract ending. The settled disposition of one habitually given to prayer.
biblical_def: Prayerfulness is the settled disposition of a soul habitually turned to God in prayer — not occasional petition but sustained communion. Paul commands it as continuing instant in prayer and pray without ceasing; Daniel modeled it as three times a day, on his knees, by an open window in defiance of decree.
webster_summary: The state or character of being given to prayer; habitual prayer.
webster_full: PRAYERFUL, adj. Given to prayer; using much prayer.
Prayerfulness names not the act of one prayer but the disposition behind a thousand — the soul that, by habit, turns toward God in matters small and great.
scriptures: Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer.
He kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God.
Men ought always to pray, and not to faint.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often outsources prayer to the platform-level (worship leaders, recordings, conferences); Scripture commands the household and individual to recover the habit.
corruption_paragraphs: Pray without ceasing (1 Thess 5:17) is not a literal command to never stop verbalizing. It is a disposition: a heart turned toward God so habitually that the smallest matter occasions prayer and the largest finds it already prepared.
Recovery is repetition. Daniel's three times a day; the morning prayer at the kitchen sink; the brief silent ‘Lord, help’ before the difficult conversation. Build the habit; the disposition follows.
roots_summary: Greek proseuchomai (to pray) and adialeiptōs (without intermission) form the Pauline command.
roots_lines: Greek proseuchomai — to pray; the standard New Testament verb.
Greek adialeiptōs — without intermission; the ‘without ceasing’ of 1 Thess 5:17.
usage: Pray without ceasing is a disposition, not a transcript.
Daniel built the habit; the disposition followed.
Always to pray and not to faint — Christ's phrasing remains.

etymology: Old English þancian (to think, give thanks) with abstract ending. The disposition of recognized gift — the soul that does not assume it is owed.
biblical_def: Thankfulness is the saint's disposition of recognized gift — the standing acknowledgment that what one has is given. Paul commands it as in every thing give thanks and grounds it in Christ: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. Thanklessness is named in 2 Timothy 3 as a mark of the perilous last days.
webster_summary: The state of being thankful; expression of gratitude; acknowledgment of a benefit received.
webster_full: THANKFUL, adj. Grateful; impressed with a sense of kindness received and ready to acknowledge it.
Scripture commands thankfulness across all conditions (Eph 5:20; 1 Thess 5:18; Phil 4:6); the assumption is that the saint is, in every state, the recipient of more grace than he has yet recognized.
scriptures: In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.
Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful.
corruption_summary: Modern entitlement culture treats gifts as owed; Scripture treats every breath as gift, and thanklessness as a perilous-last-days symptom.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 1 traces the Gentile fall: when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful (Rom 1:21). Thanklessness is the second step in the cosmic descent. The whole pagan disorder follows.

The household's daily practice of thanksgiving — verbal, before meals, in evening prayer, in trial — is therefore not decorative. It is one of the load-bearing disciplines of a life that does not slide. Recognized gift sustains; assumed entitlement corrodes.
roots_summary: Greek eucharistia (thanksgiving) gives us Eucharist; the same root.
roots_lines: Greek eucharistia — thanksgiving; giving of thanks.
Note: same root behind charis (grace); thankfulness is the soul's recognition of grace.
usage: Thanklessness is a perilous-last-days symptom; recognize it.
In every thing give thanks — that is God's will, expressly stated.
The Eucharist is thanksgiving; do not skip the meaning.

etymology: Old English halignes, related to hal (whole). The state of being set apart and rendered whole.
biblical_def: Holiness is the state of being set apart unto God and rendered whole — both granted in Christ (1 Cor 1:30) and pursued by the saint (Heb 12:14: follow... holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord). It is positional and practical at once: declared in justification, worked out in sanctification.
webster_summary: The state of being holy; purity or integrity of moral character; freedom from sin; sanctity.
webster_full: HOLINESS, n. The state of being holy; purity of moral character; sanctity; freedom from sin.

Scripture has both an objective and a subjective sense: God Himself is holy (Isa 6:3); His people are made holy in Christ (1 Cor 1:30); His people pursue holiness practically (Heb 12:14; 1 Pet 1:15-16).
scriptures: Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.
But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation.
Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy.
I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often treats holiness as either automatic (already imputed) or impossible (only future); Hebrews 12:14 commands its present pursuit.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 12:14 is uncompromising: follow holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord. The verse does not earn salvation; it describes the necessary trajectory of the genuinely saved.

1 Peter 1:15-16 grounds the pursuit in God's own character: be ye holy; for I am holy. Holiness is a family resemblance — the children look like the Father over time. The saint pursues; the Spirit grows the resemblance.
roots_summary: Hebrew qadosh and Greek hagios — both mean ‘set apart, holy’.
roots_lines: Hebrew qadosh — holy, set apart; the LORD is the Holy One of Israel.
Greek hagios — holy, set apart; New Testament saints are hagioi (holy ones).
usage: Follow holiness; without it no man shall see the Lord.
Be ye holy, for I am holy — the family resemblance.
Holiness is positional and pursued; both, not either.

etymology: Old English godnes; in Scripture, the active beneficence and moral wholeness that flows from God and characterizes the saint who walks with Him.
biblical_def: Biblical goodness is the active beneficence and moral wholeness God displays toward His creatures and produces in His saints. Paul lists it as fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22). David longs for it: surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life. Goodness in Scripture is never passive; it acts.
webster_summary: The state of being good; the moral quality of doing right and acting beneficently.
webster_full: GOODNESS, n. The state of being good; moral excellence; benevolence in actions; kindness in disposition.
Scripture distinguishes chrēstotēs (kindness) and agathōsynē (goodness) as related but separable virtues; both are listed in Galatians 5:22 as fruit of the Spirit.
scriptures: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith.
I myself also am persuaded of you, my brethren, that ye also are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge.
The goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance.
corruption_summary: Modern usage often pairs ‘good’ with ‘nice’; biblical goodness is closer to active beneficence and moral substance than to social pleasantness.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 23:6's goodness and mercy shall follow me uses verbs of pursuit. The Hebrew suggests they hunt the saint down. Goodness is not passive scenery; it tracks the saint into every day.

Romans 2:4 carries the deepest pastoral note: the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance. The saint repents not because God is harsh but because He is good. Recover this and the gospel sounds different: God's goodness is the engine, not His severity.
roots_summary: Greek agathōsynē covers active goodness; Hebrew tov covers the broader sense.
roots_lines: Greek agathōsynē — goodness; specifically of moral substance and beneficent action.
Hebrew tov — good; the very first adjective God applies to His creation (Gen 1:4) and the dominant Hebrew goodness-word.
usage: Goodness and mercy hunt the saint down all his days.
It is the goodness of God that leads to repentance.
Goodness is active beneficence, not social pleasantness.
